newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine lawmakers to produce report on graft.
newsitem.headline: Argentine lawmakers to produce report on graft.

text.p: A Congressional committee probing a graft scandal in Argentina's customs service will issue its first progress report Friday and call former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo to testify early January, panel members said.
"On Friday the 27th, the committee will present a report on its work to date," committee member Pedro Dufou of the opposition Radical Party told Reuters.

The panel, formed two months ago to investigate charges that some $10 billion worth of goods have been smuggled into the country over the past four years, plans to call Cavallo to testify in early January.

The former minister, credited with returning Argentina to a path of growth and currency stability, has accused two cabinet ministers of blocking corruption investigations and of manipulating judges probing graft and smuggling scandals. Both have denied the charges.

Another panel member, Gaston Mercado Luna, also a Radical, told local radio that the group expected Cavallo to present concrete evidence to substantiate his charges against Interior Minister Carlos Corach and Justice Minister Elias Jassan.
"All Argentines are expecting concrete proof," he said.

Mercado Luna said committee members have requested the impeachment of Corach and Jassan based on Cavallo's charges. The former minister has lashed out at several government officials since he was fired by President Carlos Menem in July.

"He cannot go on making daring accusations without coming up with the necessary proof to justify what he has said, in which he is necessarily an accomplice and which he lacked the guts or decisiveness to say before," Mercado Luna said.

Committee chairman Mario Das Neves of the ruling Peronist Party denied press allegations that a series of delays in summoning the former economic czar were due to government pressure, although he admitted many officials were concerned by the possibility of seeing Cavallo make more charges in Congress.

"Every time former minister Cavallo shows up, he creates a state of shock," he told local radio. Although he admitted having received a nervous call from Corach, Das Neves said the committee was free from any government pressure.
Cavallo was originally set to testify Monday, then was tentatively moved to next Thursday. Now panel members are saying he will most likely be called in early January.
"The only inconvenience is over a matter of days, that's all," Das Neves said. "(But) we will definitely call him."
